b011: A quarterly print report for the wealth division of a Vietnamese private bank, set in Vietnamese and English, needs a text face with some refinement.
b018: Mobile banking app for a Greek retail bank, interface in Greek and English. The Greek should feel as considered as the Latin rather than an afterthought, and numerals need to line up cleanly down a transaction list.
b035: We are putting a prepaid card into physical packaging and want the type to feel hard-edged and confrontational.
b051: A pitch deck for a Vietnamese consumer payments startup, presented in Vietnamese, that should come across as energetic rather than corporate.
b073: A technical whitepaper on settlement infrastructure, published in English with a Japanese translation. Readers spend the better part of an hour in it, so the Latin has to hold up across long paragraphs and sit comfortably beside the Japanese.
b086: A private bank's annual investor letter, roughly forty pages of continuous text set at 10.5pt on uncoated stock. We need old-style figures for the prose and lining tabular figures for the tables, a drawn small-caps cut for section openers, and an italic with genuine cursive structure rather than a slanted roman. It has to read as elegant without tipping into ornamental.
b091: A savings app aimed at first-time investors in Greece, interface in Greek and English. Type must stay legible at 12px on a five-inch screen, carry tabular figures so balances do not shift as they update, and place the Greek tonos correctly. The tone should feel encouraging rather than institutional, and we need at least four weights to build interface hierarchy.
b097: Card carrier and welcome pack for a business banking product, and it should read as solid and long established.
b101: A budgeting app for the Russian market, interface in Russian and English. It needs a properly drawn Cyrillic rather than a Latin face with transliterated glyphs, has to stay legible at 11px for category labels, and should offer a variable weight axis so we can animate emphasis without shipping extra files. The tone is light and encouraging, aimed at users in their twenties.
b115: Packaging for a metal credit card aimed at Russian-speaking private clients, and it should feel restrained and expensive.
b120: A Ukrainian bank's public website, in Ukrainian and English. The Cyrillic must include a correctly drawn ghe with upturn and yi, not a Russian set with substitutions. WCAG AA contrast at 16px body, tabular figures for rate tables, and a licence permitting us to self-host on our own servers. The face should read as institutional and unexcitable.
b129: A quarterly earnings deck for a listed payments company. It has to project stability when read from the back of a boardroom, and still hold together in dense appendix tables at small sizes.
b131: A remittance service for Japanese workers sending money home, site in Japanese and English, and it should feel approachable.
b137: A printed rate card for a Greek brokerage, set in Greek and English, that needs to read as precise.
b144: A Vietnamese peer-to-peer payments site aimed at students. Vietnamese diacritics stack two deep on some vowels and must not collide at 16px body. We want a display cut for the hero and a text cut for the body from the same family, plus a variable weight axis. The tone is bright and casual without being juvenile.
b149: A printed derivatives pricing manual for a Greek institution, set in Greek and English. Body runs at 9pt in two columns, so the face needs a large x-height and open apertures at that size. The Greek must include polytonic accents for the historical appendix. Tabular lining figures throughout, and a monospace companion for the formula listings.
b157: A crypto exchange aimed at Russian-speaking traders. The brand is deliberately harsh and anti-corporate, and the site is bilingual, so the Cyrillic has to carry the same aggression as the Latin rather than softening it.
b163: An internal architecture deck for a payments engineering team. Slides are dense with system diagrams and inline code, so we need something that stays readable when projected and pairs cleanly with a monospace.
b169: Packaging for a limited-run debit card released with a Japanese streetwear label. The lockup sets Latin and Japanese at the same optical size, so the Latin needs weights heavy enough not to look thin beside kanji. Foil stamping means no stroke can fall below 0.4pt at final size. The face should feel harsh and industrial.
b173: A zine-style printed annual report for a fintech with offices in Tokyo and Berlin, set in Japanese and English. It should feel raw and photocopied, and the Latin has to survive being reproduced badly on purpose.
b174: A long-form financial literacy guide in Vietnamese, read both on screen and in print. Sessions run twenty minutes or more, so it needs to stay comfortable across extended reading, and the Vietnamese diacritics must not feel cramped.
b010: A clinician-facing app for reviewing lab results mid-shift. Values are read at a glance under time pressure, so we need tabular figures, unambiguous separation of 1, l and I as well as 0 and O, and legibility at 12px on a phone held at arm's length. Four weights minimum, and a licence that permits embedding in a native app.
b019: A conference deck for a Greek medical society, presented in Greek, and it should feel dignified.
b029: Packaging for an over-the-counter children's cold remedy sold in Vietnam, labelled in Vietnamese and English, that should feel gentle and reassuring.
b065: A printed patient consent form used across a Vietnamese hospital network. It has to read as unambiguous and official, and the Vietnamese diacritics need to stay clear after the form has been photocopied several times.
b079: A Vietnamese national vaccination record app. Text must render Vietnamese correctly including stacked diacritics on uppercase, stay legible at 13px for dose names, and use tabular figures for dates and lot numbers. It has to read as official and trustworthy, and the licence must permit offline embedding, since rural clinics frequently have no connectivity.
b082: A slide deck for a hospice care fundraising evening that should feel gentle.
b102: A Russian-language clinical practice guideline, around 180 pages, read on screen as a PDF and in print. Body runs at 10pt with heavy footnoting, so we need a face with a genuine small-text optical size, Cyrillic italics that follow cursive convention rather than sloping the roman, and tabular figures for the dosage tables.
b112: A harm reduction poster campaign in Greek that needs to feel blunt and unsentimental.
b121: Packaging for a sharps disposal container used in clinical settings. Warning text must be legible at two metres and survive printing on textured polypropylene, which swallows fine detail. We need extreme weights for hazard headings, a condensed cut to fit mandated regulatory text into a fixed area, and no ambiguity between 1 and 7. The tone is deliberately stark.
b124: A deck for a joint research programme between a Tokyo hospital and a US partner, with slides in Japanese and English. The Latin needs to sit at the same visual weight as the Japanese, and the data slides carry a lot of small numerals.
b134: A commemorative printed history of a Russian teaching hospital, set in Russian with English captions at 11pt on cream uncoated stock, running to about 300 pages. We need old-style figures for the prose, true italics in both scripts, small caps for the Latin, and Cyrillic drawn by someone working inside the tradition rather than adapting the Latin.
b138: Packaging for children's vitamin gummies sold in Vietnam, labelled in Vietnamese and English, that should feel fun.
b154: A private fertility clinic's website, in Greek and English. Body text at 17px with generous line height, because anxious readers scan slowly, Greek with correctly positioned tonos, at least three weights plus italics, and ideally a variable optical size axis since headings run to 48px. The feeling should be calm and refined rather than clinical.
b156: A slide deck teaching handwashing to primary school children in Japan, presented in Japanese with some English. It needs to feel friendly and animated on screen, and the Latin should not look severe beside the Japanese.
b161: Packaging for a range of children's plasters sold in Greece. Type appears small on the box in both Greek and English, and it should feel cheerful without becoming hard to read.
b177: A mobile app for a cosmetic dermatology practice. It should feel refined and unhurried, and still function as an interface with clear hierarchy at small sizes.
b185: A Japanese pharmaceutical safety dossier submitted to regulators, several hundred pages in Japanese with English abstracts. The Latin must pair with Noto Serif JP without a weight mismatch, hold up at 9pt in two columns, and provide tabular figures for the adverse event tables. Nothing decorative, and the licence has to permit redistribution inside submitted PDFs.
b194: A public health information site for a Russian-speaking population. It has to read as an official source people can trust, and the Cyrillic needs to stay legible for older readers at default browser sizes.
b201: A book-length guide for caregivers of dementia patients, published in Japanese and English, and it should feel compassionate.
b203: A blunt anti-smoking campaign site aimed at young men in Vietnam, written in Vietnamese.
b208: An illustrated health education book for Russian teenagers, written in Russian. It is read for long stretches, so it has to stay comfortable, and the tone should be light rather than lecturing.
